messages.subject: Summary for occurrence distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to get similar summary information as from AKDEs but for occurrence distributions (ODs). The summary() command when used with an OD shows errors like so:

> occur_summary_1_90 <- summary(OCCUR.85046, level.UD = 0.90, level = 0.95)
Error in if (any(I)) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

.. and when trying to use summary.UD():

> occur_summary_1_90 <- summary.UD(OCCUR.85046, level.UD = 0.90, level = 0.95)
Error in summary.UD(OCCUR.85046, level.UD = 0.9, level = 0.95) :
  could not find function "summary.UD"

This isn't the biggest deal, as I've exported my rasters and shapefiles for ArcGIS already and am proficient enough with ArcGIS to do what I'd like, but I was just wondering:

1) Is my inability to use summary() for ODs on purpose, or is there a problem with my code/R/ctmm package?

2) Does it make sense to get 50/90 contours, or any "area" calculation, for ODs? My thoughts are that since it's only giving an estimate of where the animal may have been able to go between locations, perhaps an area estimate is unnecessary.

Thanks for any feedback!

Chris

messages.subject: Re: Summary for occurrence distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I never coded a summary method for occurrence distributions because their coverage areas reflect our ignorance of where the animal was (which is sampling dependent) more than they reflect some biology that can be compared between individuals. Usually, in the literature, when people are calculating things like Brownian-bridge "home-range" areas, they are conflating occurrence distributions with range distributions.

I should code summary.UD() to say something to this effect instead of just not working.
The way to force summary() to resolve to summary.UD() would be ctmm:::summary.UD()... that isn't going to help here, though.
I don't know what you are doing in your analysis, but its likely that you don't want to be using occurrence areas. Feel free to submit questions about that.

Best,
Chris

I was initially going to record what type of habitat each of my locations were in within the device error, but then thought that perhaps using an OD would give further information. Reading your response to my first question, it seems to me that this might not be a good idea and perhaps I should stick with just looking at what habitat is inside their home ranges...

I have shown "Individual x has #% of forest block A, #% of forest block B, etc within their home range," but whether those blocks are important is what I'm trying to tease out. Any input would be greatly appreciated!

TIA!

Chris

messages.subject: Re: Summary for occurrence distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

With the occurrence distribution, you can directly obtain point estimates for what covariates the individual sampled during observation, but not with the contours. You take the PMF of the occurrence distribution and add up the probability mass within a certain habitat type to get the fraction of time spent in that habitat type. This is less safe to calculate with the KDE range estimate, which is extrapolating space use and not habitat use, however the occurrence distribution may not be representative of long-term habitat use.

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: ctmm 0.5.2 overlap, uere changes
messages.body_plain:
1) Previously, in versions 0.5.1 and below, the AKDE overlaps could either be calculated via
overlap(data_list,ctmm_list)
or
overlap(ud_list,ctmm_list)
with UDs were calculated on the same grid. As there is no real case where users want the overlaps and not the UDs, and as the fitted model is specific to the UD, AKDE overlap usage in 0.5.2 has been simplified to just
overlap(ud_list)
with no ctmm_list argument. The model fit object is now stored in a slot of the UD object.

2) Previously, in versions 0.5.1 and below, UERE estimates were calculated from calibration data via
UERE <- uere(calibration_data)
which is confusing as UERE values were assigned via
uere(data_to_calibrate) <- UERE
Starting in ctmm 0.5.2, uere() only reports how the data has been calibrated and now uere.fit() is used to estimate UERE values. So the same calibration process looks like
UERE <- uere.fit(calibration_data)
uere(data_to_calibrate) <- UERE
See, also, https://ctmm-initiative.github.io/ctmm/reference/uere.html

Best,
Chris

Dear Chris,

I have collected calibration data over 3 hours with the time interval of 10 seconds with the Canmore GT-740FL GPS device. Figure 1 shows the corresponding error autocorrelation plot for my calibration data using residuals() and correlogram() functions.

I subsampled the calibration data to 1 minute time interval and did the same procedure as above-mentioned to check the error autocorrelation of observations with 1 minute time interval.

In Figure 2 unlike Figure 1, a lot of points are within the upper and lower band drawn by the red dotted dash-lines. It means for many time lags, the error autocorrelation are statistically zero . Can I conclude that the impact of error autocorrelation is negligible for observations with 1 minute time interval? If so, What about the specific time lag of 1 minute in Figure 1 and 2? Thank you in advance,

Maryam

messages.subject: Re: Irregular gaps in GPS data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dave,

One of the major benefits of working in continuous time is that irregular sampling is not necessarily problematic. In ctmm.fit() the missing times are properly marginalized over. In akde() there is the weights option to account for irregularity (https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/eap.1704).

The variograms are more sensitive to irregularity (though they are only for visualization), and there are options for dealing with this: dt, res, and fast.

Overall, your variograms look pretty good and its hard for me to say exactly what your gaps are doing without knowing the autocorrelation structure of the gaps, but I don't think uncorrelated, short gaps will cause any major artifacts in the variograms. You can always simulate data with the same sampling schedule to see what impact there is on a known truth.

Bobcat #4 looks dispersive (male?). Bobcat #9 looks like they have a lunar cycle of some kind.

Best,
Chris
